## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is only one result so far: the starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds, so nothing yet separates network effects from recipe effects. The default recipe runs 4 epochs, which gives about 131k samples, or 32 updates. That may be too few, and the entropy setting may be too high for the precision needed to build each design exactly.

The key decision per brick is this: the brick lands one layer above the highest filled cell under its footprint. It is correct only if every cell it fills at that layer is a missing target cell and it leaves no missing target cells sealed below it. The starting pool head has to work out this layer-specific condition from per-column features, which is hard to learn from little data.

The three candidates are set up so each comparison changes one thing:
- **A** (start + recipe) against the start tests the recipe alone.
- **B** (layered head) against A tests a head that scores each layer separately.
- **C** against B tests 1 epoch versus 2 epochs.

### Round 2
All three trials scored exactly 0 on dev and on training success in the last 10% of training. That holds for both 2- and 1-epoch recipes, ~230k–430k samples, and two head designs (the per-column pooling head, and the per-layer head combined with logsumexp). Seed noise can't separate any of them, and none got even rare exact builds while training, so the failure is basic rather than a small gap. Possible causes: too few policy updates (only 59–104), the PPO batch is large; a head whose footprint alignment is fixed by hand, which could be wrong if this world numbers anchors or orientations differently; and too little global reasoning (overhangs need bridging bricks placed in the right order, and DONE needs a check over the whole grid). Next steps: (1) keep the start network and only cut the batch so there are about 4× more updates; (2) build a deeper residual 3×3 conv network with global context, a 3×3 per-type head that doesn't depend on alignment, and the legal-action mask as input; (3) a small transformer over cells with the same head. All three use the many-updates recipe.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on train, across recipes (1–4 epochs, 230k–425k steps), heads (pool, per-layer, 3x3-conv) and trunks (CNN, transformer). Seed noise cannot explain that. On small designs with no overhangs, even a weak learner should place some bricks correctly and build a few exactly. So something systematic is probably broken, and the task warns that the world may differ from its description. One thing all six share: every head assumes that the logit at flattened position (t, y, x) acts on observation cell (y, x). If the world's action indexing is transposed, flipped or permuted relative to the observation, a translation-equivariant head can never learn the mapping. This round tests that directly with three heads: a fully dense action mapping (any permutation), a dihedral-transform head that learns which flip or transpose to use (structured and sample-efficient), and a combination of the two. Recipe stays at the most-update setting.

### Round 4
Nine trials, all at 0 on both seeds and 0 train success: recipe changes (2 or 1 epochs, 59 to 208 updates), heads (footprint pooling, per-layer logsumexp, 3x3 conv, transformer, dense mixer, dihedral) and trunks all failed. A design of 6 bricks should sometimes be built by chance during training, and that never happened. This suggests a systematic mismatch, not slow learning. The world 'may not behave as described', and the likeliest hidden difference is the action layout. Spatial heads cannot learn a cell-major index (cell*n_types + type) or an x-major index (x*Y + y), and the dense head learns too slowly. Flips alone (dihedral) were already ruled out. In this last round, every candidate emits placement logits under four flatten layouts at once (type/cell-major × y/x-major) and sums them, so training can switch off the wrong ones. Each also feeds the mask in matching layouts.
